:::{#def-finite-additivity}
#### Finite additivity

A function $\mu$ that assigns a real number $\mu(A)$ to each [event](#def-event) $A$
is **finitely additive**
if, for every finite collection of
[mutually exclusive](#def-mutually-exclusive) events $A_1, \ldots, A_n$,
the value of their union is the sum of their values:

$$\mu(A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mu(A_i)$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-finite-additivity}
#### Counting outcomes is finitely additive

For the die roll in @exm-sample-space,
let $\mu(A) \eqdef \abs{A}$, the number of outcomes in $A$.
The events $\set{1, 2}$ and $\set{5, 6}$ are mutually exclusive
(@exm-mutually-exclusive), and:

$$
\ba
\mu(\set{1, 2} \cup \set{5, 6})
&= \mu(\set{1, 2, 5, 6})
&& \text{(take the union)} \\
&= 4
&& \text{(count the outcomes)} \\
&= 2 + 2
&& \text{(write 4 as a sum)} \\
&= \mu(\set{1, 2}) + \mu(\set{5, 6})
&& \text{(count each event's outcomes)}
\ea
$$

The same holds for any mutually exclusive events,
because the sizes of disjoint sets add,
so $\mu$ is finitely additive.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-countable-additivity}
#### Countable additivity

A function $\mu$ that assigns a real number $\mu(A)$ to each [event](#def-event) $A$
is **countably additive**
(also called **$\sigma$-additive**)
if, for every sequence of
[mutually exclusive](#def-mutually-exclusive) events $A_1, A_2, \ldots$,
the value of their union is the sum of their values:

$$\mu\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \mu(A_i)$$

:::

::: notes

Countable additivity implies [finite additivity](#def-finite-additivity).
Applying countable additivity to $\emptyset, \emptyset, \ldots$,
which are mutually exclusive with union $\emptyset$,
gives $\mu(\emptyset) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \mu(\emptyset)$,
a sum of identical terms that is finite only if $\mu(\emptyset) = 0$.
Then, for mutually exclusive $A_1, \ldots, A_n$,
set $A_{n+1} = A_{n+2} = \cdots = \emptyset$
and apply countable additivity to the whole sequence.
The converse fails:
there exist set functions that satisfy finite additivity
but fail countable additivity
(see [Wikipedia: Sigma-additive set function --- An additive function which is not $\sigma$-additive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma-additive_set_function#An_additive_function_which_is_not_%CF%83-additive)).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-countable-additivity}
#### Counting outcomes is countably additive

For the counting function $\mu(A) \eqdef \abs{A}$ of @exm-finite-additivity,
take any sequence of mutually exclusive events $A_1, A_2, \ldots$.
No two of them share an outcome, and $\Omega$ has only six outcomes,
so at most six of the $A_i$ contain any outcomes;
the rest are $\emptyset$, with $\mu(\emptyset) = 0$.
The infinite sum therefore has at most six nonzero terms,
and finite additivity (@exm-finite-additivity) shows that those terms
add up to $\mu$ of the union.
So $\mu$ is countably additive.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-probability}
#### Probability measure

A **probability measure** on a [sample space](#def-sample-space) $\Omega$,
often denoted $\Pr()$ or $\P()$,
is a function that assigns a number $\Pr(A)$ to each [event](#def-event) $A$
and satisfies:

1. For any event $A$, $\Pr(A) \ge 0$.
2. The probability of the whole sample space is 1:
   $$\Pr(\Omega) = 1$$
3. $\Pr$ is [countably additive](#def-countable-additivity):
   for any [mutually exclusive](#def-mutually-exclusive) events $A_1, A_2, \ldots$,
   $$\Pr\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \Pr(A_i)$$

:::

::: notes

Property 3 implies that $\Pr$ is also [finitely additive](#def-finite-additivity).
Requiring countable additivity, not just finite additivity,
enables results such as
the continuity of probability
(if $A_1 \supseteq A_2 \supseteq \cdots$ with $\bigcap_i A_i = \emptyset$,
then $\Pr(A_i) \to 0$),
and it is what makes sums over countably infinite [partitions](#def-partition) valid.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-probability}
#### Probability measure for a fair die

For the die roll in @exm-sample-space,
define $\Pr(A) \eqdef \abs{A} / 6$,
where $\abs{A}$ is the number of outcomes in $A$.
This function is non-negative, gives $\Pr(\Omega) = 6/6 = 1$,
and is [countably additive](#def-countable-additivity),
because it is $1/6$ times the counting function of @exm-countable-additivity.
The event "the roll is even" from @exm-event has probability
$\Pr(\set{2, 4, 6}) = 3/6 = 1/2$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-prob-subset}
#### Probability of a subset's intersection

If $A$ and $B$ are events and $A\subseteq B$, then $\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)$.

:::

::: proof
Since $A \subseteq B$, every outcome in $A$ is also in $B$, so $A \cap B = A$,
and therefore $\Pr(A \cap B) = \Pr(A)$.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-total-prob-1}
#### An event and its complement sum to 1

For any event $A$ and its [complement](#def-complement) $\neg A$:

$$\Pr(A) + \Pr(\neg A) = 1$$

:::

::: proof

The events $A$ and $\neg A$ are disjoint, and their union is $\Omega$.

$$
\ba
\Pr(A) + \Pr(\neg A)
&= \Pr(A \cup \neg A)
&& \text{(additivity of probability for disjoint events)} \\
&= \Pr(\Omega)
&& \text{(} A \cup \neg A = \Omega \text{)} \\
&= 1
&& \text{(probability of the sample space is 1)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-p-neg0}
#### Complement rule

For any event $A$:

$$\Pr(\neg A) = 1 - \Pr(A)$$

:::

::: proof
Subtract $\Pr(A)$ from both sides of @thm-total-prob-1.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-p-neg}
#### Complement rule in probability ($\pi$) notation

If the probability of an event $A$ is $\Pr(A)=\pi$,
then the probability that $A$ does not occur is:

$$\Pr(\neg A)= 1 - \pi$$

:::

::: proof

$$
\ba
\Pr(\neg A) &= 1 - \Pr(A)
&& \text{(complement rule)} \\
&= 1 - \pi
&& \text{(substitute } \Pr(A) = \pi \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-p-neg}
#### Probability of not rolling a six

For a fair die, the event "the roll is a six" has probability $\pi = 1/6$,
so by @cor-p-neg the probability of not rolling a six is $1 - 1/6 = 5/6$.

:::
